title: Self Hosted Workflow Automation for Government: 2026
summary: Self-hosted workflow automation for government should be evaluated by licensing, infrastructure control, and sustainability rather than feature counts.
body_markdown:
## The strongest case against self-hosting automation in government


Run your own automation servers in a small agency team and you take on patching, uptime, accreditation and staff turnover. A government cloud region run by a provider may be both safer and cheaper. That's the objection, and it's a good one.


### Why self-hosting automation burdens government staff


Under self-hosting, every operational duty moves onto people who already have other jobs.


Someone must apply security patches on a schedule, keep the service up when the workflow engine stalls, and maintain the accreditation evidence an auditor will ask for.


> Under self-hosting, every operational duty moves onto people who already have other jobs.


Someone must also hand all of it over when the one person who understands the setup leaves. In a team of three, that last item is the one that fails first.


Failure is not trivial in cost.[IBM's Cost of a Data Breach 2025, as summarised by Think Digital Partners](https://www.thinkdigitalpartners.com/news/2025/08/12/cost-of-public-sector-data-breaches-on-the-rise/) , puts the **average healthcare breach at $7.42m** , which is the highest of the sectors compared.


Financial services follow at $5.56m, energy and utilities at $5.29m, and technology at $5m, so technology companies sit well above the lowest average breach costs of the sectors analyzed. Education sits at $3.7m and retail at $3.48m.


Even the lowest figure in the set, public sector at $2.86m, is a sum most agency budgets can't absorb, so an unpatched server is a liability whichever sector's average you pick.


Across many customers, a provider with a dedicated security staff carries that risk, and the agency doesn't carry it alone.


### When a government cloud beats self-hosting automation


Only one assumption keeps the objection standing: that the data in question may sit in a government cloud region. Where it can, the provider-run option usually wins, because it removes the maintenance burden the team cannot staff.


Where residency or air-gap rules apply, the assumption fails.


If the data must stay on infrastructure the agency controls, or the network must have no outbound path, a provider region isn't a cheaper option. In that case, it's a non-compliant one, and self-hosting is the only route that passes review.


**The deciding condition is therefore a single question: does a cloud region that satisfies your residency and isolation rules exist?** If yes, use it. If no, self-host, and size the team to patch it.
